notes.Accounting concepts:
## Overview
Accounting principles make sure financial statements are prepared consistently and fairly. You need the purpose of accounting, the accounting equation, and the main concepts and policies.
## Key ideas
- **Book-keeping**: recording transactions. **Accounting**: using the records to prepare and interpret statements.
- Purpose: record transactions, calculate profit/loss, show financial position, help decisions, control assets.
- **Accounting equation**: **Assets = Capital + Liabilities**.
### Concepts
| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Business entity | Owner and business are separate |
| Duality | Every transaction has two effects (debit and credit) |
| Historic cost | Assets recorded at their cost price |
| Money measurement | Only items with a money value are recorded |
| Going concern | Business assumed to continue in the foreseeable future |
| Accruals (matching) | Income and expenses recorded in the period they relate to, not when cash is paid |
| Prudence | Do not overstate profits or assets; record losses when likely |
| Consistency | Use the same methods each year |
| Realisation | Revenue recorded when goods are transferred to the customer |
| Materiality | Small items can be treated simply (e.g. stapler as an expense) |
- Qualities of useful information: **relevance, reliability, comparability, understandability**.
- **IAS** (International Accounting Standards) give rules that make accounts comparable.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Asset | Resource owned by the business |
| Liability | Amount owed by the business |
| Capital | Owner's investment in the business |
| Drawings | Resources taken out by the owner for private use |
## Worked example
**Q: Assets $48 000, liabilities $13 000. Find capital.**
- Capital = 48 000 − 13 000 = **$35 000**
**Q: Which concept: the owner's house is not in the business accounts?**
- **Business entity**.
## Common mistakes
- Mixing up prudence and consistency.
- Recording the owner's private expenses as business expenses.
## Exam tips
- When asked to name a concept, explain it AND apply it to the situation.
notes.Double-entry bookkeeping:
## Overview
Double entry records every transaction twice — a debit in one account and a credit in another. You need the rules for assets, liabilities, capital, expenses and income, and how to balance accounts.
## Key ideas
- **Debit** = left side, **Credit** = right side.
| Account type | Increase | Decrease |
|---|---|---|
| Asset | Debit | Credit |
| Expense | Debit | Credit |
| Drawings | Debit | Credit |
| Liability | Credit | Debit |
| Capital | Credit | Debit |
| Income / revenue | Credit | Debit |
- Memory aid **DEAD CLIC**: Debit Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credit Liabilities, Income, Capital.
- **Cash sale**: Dr Cash, Cr Sales. **Credit sale**: Dr Trade receivable (customer), Cr Sales. **Credit purchase**: Dr Purchases, Cr Trade payable (supplier).
- **Returns**: sales returns (Dr Sales returns, Cr customer); purchases returns (Dr supplier, Cr Purchases returns).
- **Balancing an account**: total both sides, put the difference (balance c/d) on the smaller side, bring it down (b/d) on the opposite side.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Trade receivable | Customer who owes the business money |
| Trade payable | Supplier the business owes money to |
| Balance c/d, b/d | Balance carried down / brought down |
## Worked example
**Q: Record: owner started business with $10 000 in the bank; bought goods on credit from Ahmed $2000.**
- Bank Dr 10 000 / Capital Cr 10 000
- Purchases Dr 2000 / Ahmed Cr 2000
## Common mistakes
- Debiting sales.
- Using "Stock" for goods bought for resale — use Purchases.
## Exam tips
- Write the date and the name of the other account in each entry.
notes.Books of original entry:
## Overview
Transactions are first recorded in books of prime entry from source documents, then posted to the ledger. You need the source documents, day books, cash books and the general journal.
## Key ideas
### Source documents
- **Invoice** (credit sale/purchase), **credit note** (returns), **debit note** (request for credit), **statement of account**, **receipt**, cheque counterfoil, bank paying-in slip.
### Books of prime entry
| Book | Records |
|---|---|
| Sales journal | Credit sales (from invoices sent) |
| Purchases journal | Credit purchases (invoices received) |
| Sales returns journal | Credit notes sent |
| Purchases returns journal | Credit notes received |
| Cash book | All cash and bank transactions |
| Petty cash book | Small cash expenses |
| General journal | Everything else: opening entries, non-current asset bought on credit, corrections, irrecoverable debts, drawings of goods |
- **Trade discount**: reduction for trade customers — not recorded in the accounts. **Cash discount**: for paying early — recorded as discount allowed (expense) or received (income).
- **Two/three-column cash book**: cash and bank columns (and discount).
- **Contra entry**: cash paid into the bank or withdrawn — recorded on both sides (marked C).
- **Petty cash — imprest system**: a fixed float; at the end of the period the amount spent is reimbursed so the float is restored. Analysis columns group expenses.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Source document | Original evidence of a transaction |
| Imprest | Fixed petty cash float topped up each period |
| Contra entry | Transfer between cash and bank |
## Worked example
**Q: Petty cash imprest $200. Spent $163. How much is reimbursed?**
- **$163**, restoring the float to $200.
## Common mistakes
- Recording trade discount in the books.
- Putting a credit sale in the cash book.
## Exam tips
- Narrations are required in the general journal.
notes.Ledgers & trial balance:
## Overview
The ledger contains all accounts; the trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy. You need the divisions of the ledger, preparing a trial balance, and errors that do and don't affect it.
## Key ideas
- Ledger divisions: **sales ledger** (customers), **purchases ledger** (suppliers), **general/nominal ledger** (all others).
- **Trial balance**: list of all ledger balances — debit balances (assets, expenses, drawings) and credit balances (liabilities, capital, income). Totals should agree.
- **Errors not revealed** by a trial balance (both sides still equal): omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal, compensating.
| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Omission | Transaction not recorded at all |
| Commission | Correct type of account but wrong person's account |
| Principle | Wrong class of account (e.g. asset as expense) |
| Original entry | Wrong amount in both accounts |
| Complete reversal | Debit and credit swapped |
| Compensating | Two errors cancel out |
- Errors that do affect it: single entry, two debits, wrong addition, wrong balancing → a **suspense account** is opened.
- Correct errors with journal entries; clear the suspense account.
- Correcting errors affects profit if an income or expense account was wrong.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Trial balance | List of ledger balances to check double entry |
| Suspense account | Temporary account for a trial balance difference |
## Worked example
**Q: Repairs $500 were debited to the Machinery account. Type of error and correction?**
- **Error of principle**. Journal: Dr Repairs 500, Cr Machinery 500. Profit decreases by $500.
## Common mistakes
- Thinking an agreeing trial balance means no errors.
## Exam tips
- For each correction, say which account is debited and credited and the effect on profit.
notes.Final accounts:
## Overview
Final accounts show the profit and financial position of a business. You need the income statement and statement of financial position for a sole trader, plus incomplete records, clubs and manufacturing accounts.
## Key ideas
### Income statement
- Revenue − sales returns = net revenue.
- **Cost of sales** = opening inventory + purchases (+ carriage inwards − purchases returns) − closing inventory.
- **Gross profit** = net revenue − cost of sales.
- Add other income (discount received, rent received). Subtract expenses (wages, rent, carriage outwards, depreciation, irrecoverable debts). = **Profit for the year**.
### Statement of financial position
- **Non-current assets** (premises, equipment, vehicles — at cost less depreciation) + **current assets** (inventory, trade receivables, bank, cash, prepayments).
- **Current liabilities** (trade payables, overdraft, accruals). **Non-current liabilities** (loans over 1 year).
- **Capital**: opening capital + profit − drawings = closing capital.
- **Working capital** = current assets − current liabilities.
### Incomplete records
- **Statement of affairs**: capital = assets − liabilities. Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced.
- Use control/total accounts to find missing sales and purchases; mark-up/margin to find missing figures.
### Clubs and societies
- **Receipts and payments account** (cash summary) and **income and expenditure account** (surplus/deficit). **Accumulated fund** instead of capital. Subscriptions adjusted for accruals and prepayments.
### Manufacturing accounts
- **Prime cost** = direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses. Add factory overheads, adjust for work in progress → **production cost**.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Gross profit | Net revenue − cost of sales |
| Carriage inwards | Delivery cost on purchases (in cost of sales) |
| Carriage outwards | Delivery cost on sales (an expense) |
| Accumulated fund | Capital of a club |
## Worked example
**Q: Opening inventory 4000, purchases 26 000, closing inventory 5000, revenue 41 000. Gross profit?**
- Cost of sales = 4000 + 26 000 − 5000 = 25 000 → GP = **16 000**
## Common mistakes
- Putting carriage outwards in cost of sales.
- Showing drawings as an expense.
## Exam tips
- Use correct headings and subtotals; full titles carry marks (e.g. "Income statement for the year ended 31 December 2025").
notes.Adjustments:
## Overview
End-of-year adjustments apply the accruals and prudence concepts. You need accruals and prepayments, irrecoverable debts, the provision (allowance) for doubtful debts, and inventory valuation.
## Key ideas
### Accruals and prepayments
- **Accrued expense** (owed at year end): add to the expense; current liability.
- **Prepaid expense** (paid in advance): subtract from the expense; current asset.
- **Accrued income** (income still to receive): add; current asset. **Income received in advance**: subtract; current liability.
### Irrecoverable debts
- A customer cannot pay: Dr Irrecoverable debts, Cr customer's account. Expense in the income statement. Debt later recovered: reinstate and record the receipt.
### Provision for doubtful debts
- Estimated % of trade receivables that may not be paid (prudence).
- Increase in provision → expense; decrease → income. Statement of financial position: trade receivables − provision.
### Inventory valuation
- At the **lower of cost and net realisable value** (prudence). Damaged items reduce closing inventory.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Accrual | Expense owed but not yet paid |
| Prepayment | Expense paid in advance |
| Net realisable value | Expected selling price less costs to sell |
## Worked example
**Q: Rent paid $13 000 in the year; annual rent is $12 000. Adjustment?**
- Prepayment $1000: income statement rent = **$12 000**; current asset prepaid rent $1000.
**Q: Trade receivables $20 000; provision 5%; last year's provision $800.**
- New = 1000 → increase 200 = expense; SoFP: 20 000 − 1000 = **$19 000**
## Common mistakes
- Charging the whole provision instead of the change.
## Exam tips
- Use a T-account working for each adjusted expense.
notes.Bank reconciliation:
## Overview
A bank reconciliation statement explains the difference between the cash book bank balance and the bank statement balance.
## Key ideas
- Differences are caused by:
  - Items on the bank statement not yet in the cash book: **bank charges, interest, direct debits, standing orders, credit transfers, dishonoured cheques** → **update the cash book first**.
  - Items in the cash book not yet on the statement: **unpresented cheques** (paid out, not yet cleared), **uncredited deposits / lodgements** (paid in, not yet shown).
- Statement: balance as per **updated** cash book → add unpresented cheques → subtract uncredited deposits = balance as per bank statement (or the reverse direction).
- Purpose: find errors and omissions, detect fraud, get an up-to-date bank balance.
- Overdraft = credit balance in the cash book; a debit on the bank statement.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Unpresented cheque | Cheque issued but not yet cleared by the bank |
| Uncredited deposit | Money paid in but not yet shown on the statement |
| Dishonoured cheque | Customer's cheque not paid by their bank |
## Worked example
**Q: Updated cash book $2400 debit. Unpresented cheques $650; uncredited deposit $300. Bank statement balance?**
- 2400 + 650 − 300 = **$2750**
## Common mistakes
- Putting bank charges in the reconciliation instead of the cash book.
## Exam tips
- Always update the cash book before writing the statement.
notes.Control accounts:
## Overview
Control accounts (total accounts) summarise all customer or supplier accounts to check accuracy and find totals quickly.
## Key ideas
- **Sales ledger control account** (trade receivables):
  - Debit: opening balance, credit sales, dishonoured cheques, interest charged.
  - Credit: receipts from customers, discounts allowed, sales returns, irrecoverable debts, **contra (set-off)**; closing balance c/d.
- **Purchases ledger control account** (trade payables):
  - Debit: payments to suppliers, discounts received, purchases returns, contra; closing balance c/d.
  - Credit: opening balance, credit purchases.
- **Contra / set-off**: when a business both buys from and sells to the same firm, balances are offset.
- Uses: checks the ledger, finds errors, gives total receivables/payables quickly, helps detect fraud, provides missing figures for incomplete records.
- Sources of figures: day books (totals) and cash book.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Control account | Summary account checking the accuracy of a ledger |
| Contra entry | Setting off amounts owed to and by the same firm |
## Worked example
**Q: Opening receivables 8000; credit sales 30 000; receipts 26 000; discounts allowed 500; returns 700. Closing balance?**
- 8000 + 30 000 − 26 000 − 500 − 700 = **$10 800**
## Common mistakes
- Including cash sales.
- Including trade discount.
## Exam tips
- Remember the receivables account looks like a customer's account; payables like a supplier's.
notes.Depreciation:
## Overview
Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life (accruals concept). You need its causes, the straight-line and reducing-balance methods, the double entry, and disposals.
## Key ideas
- Causes: wear and tear, time, obsolescence, depletion.
- **Straight-line**: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life — same amount each year.
- **Reducing-balance**: fixed % of net book value — more in early years.
- **Revaluation** method (small items like loose tools): opening value + purchases − closing value.
- Double entry: Dr Depreciation (expense), Cr Provision for depreciation (accumulated). SoFP shows cost − accumulated depreciation = **net book value (NBV)**.
- **Disposal account**: Dr Disposal with cost; Cr Disposal with accumulated depreciation and sale proceeds; difference = profit or loss on disposal.
- Capital vs revenue expenditure: buying/improving non-current assets is capital; running costs and repairs are revenue.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Net book value | Cost − accumulated depreciation |
| Residual value | Expected value at end of useful life |
| Obsolescence | Asset becomes out of date |
## Worked example
**Q: Machine cost $20 000, 20% reducing balance. Depreciation for years 1 and 2?**
- Year 1: 4000 (NBV 16 000). Year 2: 20% × 16 000 = **3200**
**Q: Vehicle cost 15 000, accumulated depreciation 9000, sold for 5000.**
- NBV 6000 → **loss on disposal $1000**
## Common mistakes
- Applying reducing balance to cost every year.
## Exam tips
- Show NBV each year in a small table.
notes.Partnerships:
## Overview
A partnership has two or more owners. You need the partnership agreement, the appropriation account, capital and current accounts, and partnership financial statements.
## Key ideas
- **Partnership agreement** covers: profit/loss sharing ratio, interest on capital, interest on drawings, partners' salaries, capital each partner contributes. Without one, profits are shared equally with no interest or salaries.
- **Appropriation account** (after profit for the year):
  - Profit for the year + interest on drawings − interest on capital − partners' salaries = residual profit, shared in the agreed ratio.
- **Capital account**: fixed — only changes with new capital.
- **Current account**: credit with interest on capital, salary, share of profit; debit with drawings, interest on drawings, share of loss.
- SoFP shows each partner's capital and current account balances.
- Advantages: more capital, shared skills and workload; disadvantages: unlimited liability, shared profits, disagreements.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Appropriation account | Shows how profit is shared between partners |
| Current account | Records each partner's share of profit and drawings |
| Interest on drawings | Charge to discourage withdrawals |
## Worked example
**Q: Profit $50 000. A and B get 5% interest on capitals of $40 000 and $20 000. B gets salary $8000. Share the rest 3 : 2.**
- Interest: A 2000, B 1000. Salary B 8000. Residual = 50 000 − 11 000 = 39 000 → A **23 400**, B **15 600**
## Common mistakes
- Treating partners' salaries as an expense in the income statement.
## Exam tips
- Lay out the appropriation account clearly with subtotals.
notes.Ratio analysis:
## Overview
Ratios help users judge profitability, liquidity and efficiency, and compare with past years or other businesses.
## Key ideas
### Profitability
- **Gross margin** = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100.
- **Profit margin** = profit for the year ÷ revenue × 100.
- **Mark-up** = gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100.
- **ROCE** = profit ÷ capital employed × 100.
### Liquidity
- **Current ratio** = current assets ÷ current liabilities (≈ 2 : 1 ideal).
- **Liquid (acid test) ratio** = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities (≈ 1 : 1).
### Efficiency
- **Rate of inventory turnover** = cost of sales ÷ average inventory (times per year). Average inventory = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.
- **Trade receivables collection period** = trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365 days.
- **Trade payables payment period** = trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365 days.
- Improving: raise prices, cut costs, control stock, chase debts.
- **Limitations**: historic data, different accounting policies, inflation, ignore non-financial factors.
- **Users**: owners, managers, lenders, suppliers, employees, government, competitors.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Liquidity | Ability to pay short-term debts |
| Profitability | Ability to make profit relative to sales/capital |
| Capital employed | Total capital invested (owner's capital + non-current liabilities) |
## Worked example
**Q: Revenue 80 000, cost of sales 50 000, expenses 18 000. Find gross margin, mark-up and profit margin.**
- GP = 30 000 → margin **37.5%**; mark-up = 30 000 ÷ 50 000 = **60%**; profit = 12 000 → **15%**
## Common mistakes
- Confusing margin (on revenue) with mark-up (on cost).
## Exam tips
- After calculating, comment: compare with last year/competitor and suggest a reason.

l.md:
## In short
Accounting records and reports a business's financial transactions so owners and others can make decisions.
## Learn it
- **Book-keeping:** recording transactions in detail. **Accounting:** using those records to prepare statements and help decisions.
- Purposes: work out profit or loss, know what the business owns and owes, control cash, help planning.
## Key words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Transaction | An exchange involving money or goods |
| Profit | Income greater than expenses |
## Remember
- Book-keeping comes first; accounting uses its results.

## In short
Assets always equal liabilities plus capital.
## Learn it
- **Assets:** resources the business owns (premises, inventory, bank).
- **Liabilities:** amounts it owes (loan, trade payables).
- **Capital (owner's equity):** what the owner has invested.
- **Assets = Capital + Liabilities**
- Every transaction changes at least two items but the equation stays balanced.
## Worked example
**Assets are $50 000 and liabilities $12 000. Find capital.**
1. Capital = 50 000 − 12 000
**Answer:** $38 000
## Remember
- Drawings and losses reduce capital; profit and extra investment increase it.

l.t: Business documents and books of prime entry
l.md:
## In short
Transactions are first written in books of prime entry using business documents.
## Learn it
### Documents
- Invoice (credit sale/purchase), credit note (goods returned), debit note, statement of account, receipt, cheque counterfoil, bank statement.
### Books of prime entry
| Book | Records | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sales journal | Credit sales | Sales invoices |
| Purchases journal | Credit purchases | Purchase invoices |
| Sales returns journal | Goods returned by customers | Credit notes sent |
| Purchases returns journal | Goods returned to suppliers | Credit notes received |
| Cash book | Cash and bank | Receipts, cheques |
| General journal | Other items (non-current assets, corrections) | Memos |
- **Trade discount:** reduction for trade buyers; not recorded. **Cash discount:** for paying early; recorded.
## Remember
- Only credit transactions go in the sales and purchases journals.

## In short
Every transaction is recorded twice: a debit in one account and a credit in another.
## Learn it
### Rules
- **Debit:** increase in assets or expenses; decrease in liabilities, capital or income.
- **Credit:** increase in liabilities, capital or income; decrease in assets or expenses.
- Memory aid **DEAD CLIC**: Debit — Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credit — Liabilities, Income, Capital.
### Examples
- Bought goods on credit from Ali: Dr Purchases, Cr Ali.
- Paid rent by cash: Dr Rent, Cr Cash.
- Owner took cash for personal use: Dr Drawings, Cr Cash.
### Balancing an account
- Add the larger side, put the difference as **balance c/d**, then bring it down as **balance b/d**.
## Remember
- Write the name of the other account in the details column.

l.t: The cash book and petty cash
l.md:
## In short
The cash book records cash and bank transactions. Petty cash handles small payments.
## Learn it
### Three-column cash book
- Columns: discount, cash, bank on each side.
- **Contra entry:** moving money between cash and bank (marked "C").
### Petty cash (imprest system)
- A fixed float is given to the petty cashier.
- Small expenses are paid and recorded in analysis columns.
- At the end of the period, the amount spent is refilled to bring it back to the float.
## Remember
- Discount allowed (debit side) and discount received (credit side) totals are posted to the ledger.

## In short
Ledgers hold the accounts. Each ledger groups a type of account.
## Learn it
- **Sales ledger:** accounts of credit customers (trade receivables).
- **Purchases ledger:** accounts of credit suppliers (trade payables).
- **General (nominal) ledger:** all other accounts — expenses, income, assets, capital.
## Remember
- A customer's account balance is a debit balance; a supplier's is a credit balance.

## In short
A trial balance lists all ledger balances to check that debits equal credits.
## Learn it
### Trial balance
- Debit balances: assets, expenses, drawings. Credit balances: liabilities, capital, income.
### Errors that do not affect the totals
- **Omission:** not recorded at all.
- **Commission:** right type of account, wrong person.
- **Principle:** wrong type of account (e.g. asset as expense).
- **Original entry:** wrong amount in both entries.
- **Complete reversal:** debit and credit swapped.
- **Compensating:** two errors cancel out.
### Errors that do affect the totals
- Single-sided entries, wrong amounts on one side, casting errors.
### Suspense account
- Used when the trial balance does not agree; corrected with journal entries.
## Remember
- Memory aid "OCPORC" for errors not revealed.

## In short
A bank reconciliation explains differences between the cash book and the bank statement.
## Learn it
### Step 1: Update the cash book
- Add credit transfers, interest received. Deduct bank charges, standing orders, direct debits, dishonoured cheques.
### Step 2: Reconciliation statement
- Start with the bank statement balance.
- Add **uncredited deposits** (lodgements not yet shown).
- Deduct **unpresented cheques**.
- The result should equal the updated cash book balance.
## Remember
- Bank statements show the bank's view: your money is a **credit** balance there.

## In short
Control accounts check the accuracy of the sales and purchases ledgers in total.
## Learn it
### Sales ledger control account (debit side)
- Opening balance, credit sales, dishonoured cheques.
### Credit side
- Cash/cheques received, discount allowed, sales returns, irrecoverable debts, contras.
### Purchases ledger control account
- Credit side: opening balance, credit purchases. Debit side: payments, discount received, purchases returns, contras.
### Uses
- Find errors quickly, give totals for the trial balance, reduce fraud.
## Remember
- Cash sales and cash purchases never go in control accounts.

## In short
Capital expenditure buys or improves non-current assets. Revenue expenditure is day-to-day running costs.
## Learn it
- **Capital expenditure:** buying a delivery van, extending a building, legal fees and installation for new machinery.
- **Revenue expenditure:** fuel, repairs, wages, insurance.
- **Capital receipts:** sale of non-current assets, loans. **Revenue receipts:** sales, rent received.
- Wrong treatment changes profit and asset values.
## Remember
- Repairs are revenue; improvements are capital.

## In short
Income and expenses must match the period they belong to.
## Learn it
- **Accrued expense:** owed but not paid → add to the expense; current liability.
- **Prepaid expense:** paid in advance → subtract from the expense; current asset.
- **Accrued income:** earned but not received → current asset.
- **Income received in advance:** current liability.
## Worked example
**Rent paid in the year is $11 000. $1 000 is still owed. Find the rent expense.**
1. 11 000 + 1 000
**Answer:** $12 000 in the income statement
## Remember
- This follows the **matching (accruals) principle**.

## In short
Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life.
## Learn it
### Causes
- Wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence, using up (depletion).
### Methods
- **Straight-line:** (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. Same each year.
- **Reducing balance:** % of net book value each year. Higher at the start.
- **Revaluation:** for small items like tools.
### Recording
- Dr Depreciation (expense), Cr Provision for depreciation.
- **Disposal account:** transfer cost and accumulated depreciation; compare with proceeds to find profit or loss on disposal.
## Worked example
**A van costs $20 000; residual value $4 000; life 4 years. Find the yearly straight-line depreciation.**
1. (20 000 − 4 000) ÷ 4
**Answer:** $4 000 per year
## Remember
- Net book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.

## In short
Some customers never pay. Inventory must be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
## Learn it
### Irrecoverable debts
- Write off: Dr Irrecoverable debts, Cr Customer account.
- **Recovered debt:** reinstate the debt, then record the receipt.
- **Provision for doubtful debts:** an estimate; only the **change** in provision goes to the income statement.
### Inventory valuation
- Value at **lower of cost and net realisable value** (prudence).
- NRV = expected selling price − costs to sell.
## Remember
- Trade receivables in the statement of financial position are shown less the provision.

## In short
A sole trader prepares an income statement and a statement of financial position.
## Learn it
### Income statement
- Revenue (less returns)
- Less cost of sales: opening inventory + purchases (+ carriage inwards − returns) − closing inventory
- = **Gross profit**
- Add other income; less expenses
- = **Profit for the year**
### Statement of financial position
- Non-current assets (at net book value)
- Current assets: inventory, trade receivables, prepaid, bank, cash
- Current liabilities: trade payables, accrued expenses, overdraft
- Non-current liabilities: long-term loans
- Capital: opening capital + profit − drawings
## Remember
- Carriage inwards goes in cost of sales; carriage outwards is an expense.

## In short
Partnership profits are shared using an appropriation account.
## Learn it
- **Partnership agreement:** capital, profit-sharing ratio, salaries, interest on capital and drawings.
- If no agreement: equal profit share, no salaries, no interest on capital.
### Appropriation account
- Profit for the year + interest on drawings − interest on capital − partners' salaries = residual profit shared in the ratio.
### Capital and current accounts
- **Capital account:** fixed capital. **Current account:** salaries, interest, share of profit, drawings.
## Remember
- Interest on drawings increases the profit available to share.

## In short
Different organisations prepare different statements.
## Learn it
### Clubs and societies
- **Receipts and payments account:** summary of cash.
- **Income and expenditure account:** surplus or deficit.
- **Accumulated fund** replaces capital.
- Subscriptions: adjust for in arrears and in advance.
### Manufacturing accounts
- Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses.
- Add factory overheads; adjust for work in progress → **cost of production**.
### Limited companies
- Share capital (ordinary and preference shares), retained earnings, general reserve.
- Dividends are paid from retained earnings.
## Remember
- Clubs do not make "profit"; they make a surplus.

## In short
When full records are not kept, missing figures are worked out.
## Learn it
- Find opening capital with a **statement of affairs**: assets − liabilities.
- Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced.
- Use control accounts to find credit sales and purchases.
- Use **mark-up** and **margin**: mark-up is profit ÷ cost; margin is profit ÷ selling price.
## Worked example
**Cost of sales is $40 000 and the mark-up is 25%. Find revenue.**
1. Gross profit = 25% × 40 000 = 10 000
2. Revenue = 40 000 + 10 000
**Answer:** $50 000
## Remember
- Do not mix up mark-up and margin.

## In short
Ratios measure profitability, liquidity and efficiency.
## Learn it
### Profitability
- Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100
- Profit margin = profit ÷ revenue × 100
- Return on capital employed = profit ÷ capital employed × 100
- Mark-up = gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100
### Liquidity
- Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (about 2 : 1 is safe)
- Liquid (acid test) ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities
### Efficiency
- Rate of inventory turnover = cost of sales ÷ average inventory
- Trade receivables turnover (days) = trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365
- Trade payables turnover (days) = trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365
## Remember
- Always compare with a previous year or another business.

## In short
Use ratios to explain how well a business is doing and suggest improvements.
## Learn it
- Falling gross margin: higher purchase costs, lower selling prices.
- Falling liquidity: too much inventory, slow customers, more short-term debts.
- Improve: raise prices, find cheaper suppliers, cut expenses, collect debts faster.
- **Limitations:** past data, different accounting policies, inflation, no non-financial factors.
- **Users:** owners, managers, lenders, suppliers, employees, government.
## Remember
- In comparisons, name the year or business that is better and say why.

## In short
Accounting principles make financial statements reliable and comparable.
## Learn it
| Principle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Business entity | Business and owner are separate |
| Duality | Every transaction has two effects |
| Going concern | Business will continue |
| Historic cost | Assets recorded at what they cost |
| Matching (accruals) | Income and expenses in the period they belong to |
| Money measurement | Only items with a money value are recorded |
| Prudence | Do not overstate profits or assets |
| Realisation | Revenue recorded when goods pass to the customer |
| Consistency | Same methods each year |
| Materiality | Small items need not be treated strictly |
### Policies
- Comparability, relevance, reliability, understandability.
## Remember
- Name the principle and explain how it applies in the question.
